text: What number, that I would say first, would feel insulting to you?
evaluation: Negotiation prep — for self-questioning. Knowing your insult floor protects against capitulation. Not for use as the opener with the other side.

text: What number, that I would say first, would feel suspicious in your favour?
evaluation: Sometimes the over-offer is a flag. Knowing the upper edge of plausibility prepares you to ask 'what's the catch'.

text: What is the number I would walk away over?
evaluation: Have it written before the conversation. Negotiating without a walkaway is hoping.

text: What is the non-money thing I would walk away over?
evaluation: Title, scope, location, manager, mission. Money is rarely the only walkaway.

text: What is the non-money thing I would accept less money for?
evaluation: Force the trade. People who can't name one usually overweight money in the heat of negotiation.

text: What is the non-money thing I would accept more money in lieu of, even if I'd prefer the thing?
evaluation: Calibration. Knowing your conversion rate matters.

text: What is my counterpart's strongest reason to want me, that I have not made explicit?
evaluation: Explicit value beats hinted value. Write the sentence; say it out loud once.

text: What is my counterpart's strongest reason to walk, that I have not addressed?
evaluation: Address it before they say it. Pre-empted objections lose half their force.

text: What does my counterpart get in trouble for, internally, by saying yes to me?
evaluation: Help them with the internal sale. Most counterparts are not the only decision-maker.

text: What does my counterpart get rewarded for, internally, by saying yes to me?
evaluation: Even better. Frame the ask in terms of their reward, not just your need.

text: What is my best alternative if this conversation fails?
evaluation: The honest BATNA, not the polished one. If it's poor, fix it before negotiating, not during.

text: What is their best alternative if this conversation fails?
evaluation: If their alternative is weaker than yours, you have leverage you may be afraid to use.

text: What would I be willing to put in writing, that they would be afraid to put in writing?
evaluation: Asymmetric specificity is a tactic. Use it carefully and only on the verifiable.

text: What would I want in writing from them that they will resist, and how will I push?
evaluation: Verbal commitments age badly. Identify the must-have written items in advance.

text: What is one piece of leverage I have not yet named, even to myself?
evaluation: Common: outside offers, internal sponsors, their timeline, scarcity of the skill, transition cost.

text: What is one piece of leverage they have over me that I have been minimising?
evaluation: Honest self-account. Visa status, runway, exclusivity, sole-offer status, emotional attachment.

text: What sentence, said calmly, would shift the conversation in my favour?
evaluation: Have one. Don't improvise the pivot. 'Help me understand how you arrived at this number' is a useful template.

text: What sentence, said calmly, would I regret saying for the rest of the relationship?
evaluation: Negotiations end; relationships continue. Don't burn what you'll need next year.

text: What is the right tone for me, given my actual position?
evaluation: Tone misfit costs deals. Confident from a strong position. Curious from a weak one. Never the reverse.

text: What is the right tone for them, that I should not match if it goes wrong?
evaluation: Pre-decide. Don't let their escalation set yours.

text: What information am I asking for that I would refuse to give, in their position?
evaluation: If your ask is one you wouldn't grant, expect resistance. Soften or strengthen accordingly.

text: What information are they likely to ask for that I should not volunteer?
evaluation: Salary history, current offer details, urgency, life circumstances. Decide in advance, not in the moment.

text: What is the smallest concession that would unblock the deal, in their eyes, that costs me least?
evaluation: Asymmetric concessions are how good deals get unstuck. Find the cheap-to-give-expensive-to-get items.

text: What is the smallest concession from them that would unblock the deal, in my eyes, that costs them least?
evaluation: Frame your ask this way and they're more likely to grant it.

text: What am I afraid will happen if I ask for what I actually want?
evaluation: The fear is usually the punishment for asking, not the no. Naming it shrinks it.

text: What is the actual, modeled probability of that bad thing happening?
evaluation: Forces a number. Often the modeled probability is far below the felt probability.

text: What would I think of a friend who took the deal I am about to take?
evaluation: Externalising the judgement reveals the real read on the deal. Use sparingly but honestly.

text: What would I think of a friend who walked away from the deal I am about to walk away from?
evaluation: Counterpart. Walking away can be wise or fearful; the friend frame catches the difference.

text: What is the part of the offer I am over-weighting because it is concrete?
evaluation: Base salary often, signing bonus sometimes. Anchor traps. Notice them.

text: What is the part of the offer I am under-weighting because it is uncertain?
evaluation: Equity, growth, manager fit, learning. Discount, but don't ignore.

text: What is the part of the offer I am over-weighting because it sounds prestigious?
evaluation: Title vanity. Brand vanity. Real cost rarely matches felt benefit.

text: What is the part of the offer I am under-weighting because it doesn't sound impressive at parties?
evaluation: Hours, commute, autonomy, sleep. The unimpressive answers are often the deciders.

text: What does my future self, in two years, want me to say in this conversation?
evaluation: Time-shift the audience. Often clarifies which short-term comfort is being bought at long-term cost.

text: What does my future self, in five years, want me to refuse in this conversation?
evaluation: Refusals deserve their own forecasting. Some yeses today are no's later, expensively.

text: What is the version of me I'd like to bring to this negotiation, in three adjectives?
evaluation: Calm, prepared, curious are common. Aggressive rarely the right choice. Pre-decide.

text: What is the version of me I am most likely to slip into under pressure?
evaluation: Self-knowledge of regression. Many people apologise into the offer or get sharp into the offer. Both lose money.

text: What is the silence I am most afraid of, and what will I not fill it with?
evaluation: Silence after an ask is gold. Don't fill it. Practice. Pre-commit.

text: What is the silence they are most likely to use on me, and how will I respond?
evaluation: Mirror or wait. Don't escalate. The first to speak after a silence usually loses ground.

text: What is one number I want to say that I have not yet said out loud, even alone?
evaluation: Say it. The number you can say in the mirror is the floor of what you can say to a counterpart.

text: What is the question I will ask if they will not name a number?
evaluation: 'What is the band for this role?' or 'What did the last person at this level get on entry?' Have one ready.

text: What is the question I will ask if they name a number that disappoints me?
evaluation: 'Help me understand how you arrived at that' is almost always better than a counter-number on the spot.

text: What is the question I will ask if they name a number that surprises me upward?
evaluation: Don't accept too fast. 'Thank you — I'd like to come back in 24 hours with my response' is honest and prudent.

text: What concession will I lead with, that signals seriousness without revealing my floor?
evaluation: Sequence matters. Concede on something they value more than you do, early.

text: What concession will I refuse to lead with, even if asked, because it sets the wrong precedent?
evaluation: Title, autonomy, scope, equity floor. Leading concessions on these signals weakness.

text: What is the deadline I want them to feel, and how will I create it without lying?
evaluation: Real deadlines beat fake ones. Honest framing: 'I owe another party an answer by Friday' is true if it is, and useful.

text: What is the deadline they want me to feel, and how will I refuse to feel it?
evaluation: Deadline pressure is a tactic. Naming it gently — 'I won't have a considered answer by then' — defuses it.

text: What is one thing that, if true about me, would cost them a lot to find out later?
evaluation: Disclose. The cost of being caught compounds. Reputation is the asset that survives the deal.

text: What is one thing that, if true about them, would cost me a lot to find out later?
evaluation: Diligence. Ask references. Look at the last three departures from the role. Read the contract.

text: What is one detail in the written terms I have not understood and have been embarrassed to ask?
evaluation: Vesting cliffs, change-of-control, non-compete, golden handcuffs, severance triggers. Ask. Always.

text: What is one detail in the written terms I understand and quietly accept that I should renegotiate?
evaluation: Common: notice period asymmetry, IP assignment scope, non-solicit duration. Ask for symmetric clauses where possible.

text: What is one outcome that would be a mutual win, that I have not proposed because it feels too generous?
evaluation: Generous proposals from a strong position often unlock surprising acceptance.

text: What is one outcome that would be a mutual loss, that I have been quietly drifting toward?
evaluation: Inertia is its own negotiator. Spot the lose-lose drift early; usually one honest sentence corrects it.

text: What is one fact about market rates I have not verified, that I am citing in my head?
evaluation: Verify. Three sources. Don't anchor on a salary site number alone.

text: What is one fact about my own performance I have not put on paper, that I will rely on in this conversation?
evaluation: Write the brag doc. Specific outcomes, dates, numbers. Memory under pressure is unreliable.

text: What is one piece of leverage I am tempted to use that would feel cheap afterward?
evaluation: Threats, ultimatums, fake competing offers. Cheap leverage corrodes the relationship even when it works.

text: What is one piece of leverage I am refusing to use that would be ethical and effective?
evaluation: Real competing offer, time pressure that's true, naming the cost of replacement. Use what's clean.

text: What is the question I am most afraid they will ask me, and what is my honest, prepared answer?
evaluation: Pre-write the honest answer. Honest beats clever. Practiced beats spontaneous.

text: What is the question I most want to ask them that I have been afraid to?
evaluation: Ask. Real signal: the question that scares you is usually the one that matters.

text: What is one thing they have already conceded, that I should not negotiate further?
evaluation: Don't punish a yes by re-litigating. Mark concessions; move on.

text: What is one thing I have already conceded that, on reflection, I should reopen?
evaluation: Reopening is costly. Do it once, with one clear reason, and not at the eleventh hour.

text: What in this deal would I happily explain to my mother?
evaluation: The plain-language test. If it's hard to explain to a non-expert, that's a flag.

text: What in this deal would I dread explaining to my mother?
evaluation: Dread is data. Investigate the dread, even briefly.

text: What is one belief about this counterparty that may be a story rather than a fact?
evaluation: We narrativise the other side. 'They will never go above X' is sometimes a story.

text: What is one belief about myself that may be costing me money in this conversation?
evaluation: 'I'm lucky to be here.' 'They might rescind.' 'It's rude to ask.' Beliefs become numbers.

text: What is one practice I will do in the 30 minutes before this call?
evaluation: Walk. Eat. Drink water. Reread the brag doc. Don't doom-scroll comparisons.

text: What is one practice I will do in the 30 minutes after this call, regardless of how it goes?
evaluation: Write the notes. Capture what was said, what wasn't, and what surprised you. Memory degrades fast.

text: What is the smallest, easiest yes I can give them that costs me nothing?
evaluation: Open with one. Reciprocity is real. Just don't mistake it for the actual concession.

text: What is the smallest, easiest yes they can give me that costs them nothing?
evaluation: Ask for one early. Builds momentum and a record of agreement before the hard items.

text: What in this deal will be hardest to renegotiate later, and have I priced that in now?
evaluation: Title, equity grant, signing bonus, level of role, manager. Hard to revisit. Get them right entering.

text: What in this deal will be easy to renegotiate later, and should I therefore not fight over now?
evaluation: Some perks, working location flex, scope. Letting the small ones pass preserves capital for the hard ones.

text: What is the relationship I am protecting in this negotiation, and is it worth the protection?
evaluation: Sometimes yes — long careers are small worlds. Sometimes no — protection becomes self-deletion.

text: What is the relationship I am over-protecting in this negotiation, that is costing me something I will resent later?
evaluation: Resentment is the price tag. Notice it before you sign.

text: What did I give up in my last negotiation that I would not give up again?
evaluation: Memory of last time. Don't repeat the same loss.

text: What did I win in my last negotiation by accident, that I should win on purpose this time?
evaluation: Lucky wins are unstable. Make the move replicable.

text: What is one fact about the company's finances I should have looked up that I haven't?
evaluation: Filings, recent funding, layoffs, runway, business model unit economics. Five minutes saves months.

text: What is one fact about the team's history I should have looked up that I haven't?
evaluation: Tenure, departures, internal moves. The graveyard tells the truth that the careers page won't.

text: What is one piece of advice I would give a friend in my position that I have been refusing to give myself?
evaluation: Often the cleanest answer of the prep. Externalise yourself; you give better counsel.

text: What is one piece of advice I have been getting that I have been overweighting because I trust the source?
evaluation: Trusted advisors have biases too — risk aversion, scarcity mindset, dated frames. Calibrate.

text: What is the cost of saying no, in months of my life, honestly?
evaluation: Force a number. Often the runway is longer than felt; sometimes shorter. Both inform the decision.

text: What is the cost of saying yes, in years of my life, honestly?
evaluation: Counterpart. Some yeses cost years that the offer cannot price in.

text: What conversation, that I am not in, is happening about me right now?
evaluation: Hiring committees, partner discussions, board reviews. Imagine the room. Adjust accordingly without paranoia.

text: What conversation, that I should be in, am I not asking to join?
evaluation: Ask. 'I'd like to talk to my potential peer before we close' is reasonable and rare.

text: What is the version of this deal that exists six months in, that I should imagine now?
evaluation: Future-state visualisation. The honeymoon ends. What does the working week look like at that point?

text: What is the version of this deal that exists three years in, that I should be honest about?
evaluation: Long horizon. Compounding good or bad. The terms now compound.

text: What is the smallest, most honest signal I want to send in this negotiation about who I am?
evaluation: Negotiations are auditions. Choose the signal you want to send and let it shape your moves.

text: What is one signal I have been sending unintentionally that I want to stop?
evaluation: Apologetic emails. Fast acceptance. Hedging language. Audit the prior thread.

text: What is the right number of times to follow up if they go silent, and over what period?
evaluation: Two follow-ups, spaced. After that, the silence is the answer. Match the cadence to the seriousness of the deal.

text: What is the wrong number of times to follow up, and what does over-following say?
evaluation: Daily nudges read as desperation regardless of merit. Pre-set the cadence in your calendar.

text: What is the right tone if I am the one who has to walk away?
evaluation: Warm, specific, brief. Leave the door open for next time. Most industries are smaller than you think.

text: What is the right tone if they are the ones who walk away?
evaluation: Same. Don't argue the rejection. A clean response often produces the second-chance call months later.

text: What is the difference between fair and good, in this deal?
evaluation: Fair is what they would offer anyone equivalent. Good is what they would offer to keep you specifically. Don't conflate.

text: What is the difference between good and best, in this deal?
evaluation: The 'best' line is rarely worth the cost in goodwill. Often 'good' is enough; sometimes 'best' is the real ask.

text: What part of this negotiation am I treating as a battle that is actually a collaboration?
evaluation: The frame leaks. Adversarial framing produces adversarial outcomes; collaborative framing usually produces better deals for both sides.

text: What part of this negotiation am I treating as a collaboration that is actually a battle?
evaluation: The opposite mistake. Some counterparts are not on your side. Notice the signals; don't naively trust.

text: What signal of bad faith would change my approach immediately, if I saw it?
evaluation: Pre-decide. Reneged terms, missing data, last-minute swaps, multiple-offer plays. Have a tripwire.

text: What signal of good faith have I already seen that I should be giving back?
evaluation: Reciprocity. Even small mirroring — promptness, clarity, written confirmations — compounds trust.

text: What is the one sentence I want to write in my journal the day this is signed?
evaluation: Compose the sentence first. Negotiate to make it true.

text: What is the one sentence I would dread writing in my journal the day this is signed?
evaluation: Counterpart. Avoid producing the conditions for that sentence.

text: What is one thing about my own value I am still discovering, that this deal is asking me to claim?
evaluation: Negotiations are also self-exposure. The number you can ask for is the number you have come to believe you are worth.

text: What is the next move, in one sentence, after this conversation ends?
evaluation: Closing. Have it written before you start. The move that follows is part of the deal.
